title: "Unit 2: ABO, H and Secretor Blood Group Systems"

## Core concepts

The supplied lecture introduces ABO codominance, genotype–phenotype relationships, blood group antigen patterns and the genetic roles of the H and secretor loci.

## ABO inheritance

A and B are codominant, while the common O allele is recessive. Examples from the unit:

| Genotype | Expected ABO phenotype |
|---|---|
| AA or AO | A |
| BB or BO | B |
| AB | AB |
| OO | O |

## ABO phenotype and antibodies

| ABO group | A/B antigens on RBCs | Expected naturally occurring plasma antibodies |
|---|---|---|
| A | A | Anti-B |
| B | B | Anti-A |
| AB | A and B | Neither anti-A nor anti-B |
| O | Neither A nor B | Anti-A and anti-B |

*This simplified table does not replace full pretransfusion compatibility testing.*

## H and secretor loci

The Unit 2 slides distinguish the **ABO locus (chromosome 9)** from the **H locus/FUT1 (chromosome 19)**. H antigen provides the precursor for A or B antigen expression on RBCs. The **FUT2 secretor locus** influences expression in secretions. The Bombay phenotype illustrates the importance of the H antigen pathway.

## Exercises

1. Predict possible offspring blood groups from parents with genotypes AO and BO.
2. Why can a deficiency of H antigen disrupt normal ABO typing assumptions?
3. Distinguish ABO, H and secretor loci in terms of the product and location of expression.
4. Explain why forward and reverse grouping are interpreted together.
